CLIP: classifying images it was never trained to classify¶

The question: an ordinary image classifier learns a fixed list of classes (the ten CIFAR-10 objects) and can say nothing else. CLIP, trained on 400 million image-caption pairs from the internet, learns something different: to place a picture and a sentence about it close together in one shared space. To classify with it you simply write the class names as sentences ("a photo of a cat.") and pick the sentence closest to the picture. That is zero-shot classification: no training image of the target dataset was ever shown. How good is it? Does it work in a domain unlike the internet photos (satellite images)? Does the wording of the sentence matter? How many labelled images does it take before an ordinary classifier on CLIP's features overtakes it? What does fine-tuning buy, and what does it cost in general ability and in robustness? We test on CIFAR-10 (everyday objects) and EuroSAT (satellite land-use tiles), where every answer is checked against the true label.

How this notebook works. Each section starts with a plain-English explanation, then the code, then a "how to read this" note.

Run it: uv run jupyter lab CV/multimodal-clip-zero-shot/multimodal_clip_zero_shot.ipynb, or Run All in any Jupyter. The two image sets (about 350 MB) and CLIP (about 600 MB) download themselves on the first run. It uses a GPU if present and takes about 15 minutes on one.

1. 💡 The simple analogy¶

Imagine a museum guide who has read millions of picture captions but has never been taught your quiz.

  • Zero-shot: you hand the guide ten cards, each with a sentence ("a photo of a cat", "a photo of a ship"...), and a photograph. She does not need training: she picks the card whose sentence best matches the picture, because she has seen similar pictures next to similar words millions of times.
  • Her blind spots: show her a satellite photograph and her experience runs out: "annual crop land" and "permanent crop land" look alike on her cards. She is also sensitive to how you word the card: "a satellite photo of a forest" works better than "forest".
  • Learning a little more (a linear probe): show her a few labelled examples of your own, and she learns what your classes look like.
  • Fine-tuning (going back to school): more intensive training makes her much better at your quiz, but she may forget some of what she knew about everyday pictures, and a drilled student can be thrown by scratches and smudges she never saw during practice.

2. Setup¶

What: imports and named constants. Why: one place for numbers like the seed, the number of training images per class in the learning curve (1 to 1,000), the fine-tuning budget (64 images per class, 5 epochs, a small learning rate) and the number of seeds (3) keeps the notebook reproducible and avoids "magic numbers". The model is openai/clip-vit-base-patch32.

def fmt_p(p: float) -> str:
    """Formats a p-value, showing values below floating-point precision honestly.

    Args:
        p: The p-value.

    Returns:
        A short string such as ``3.2e-08`` or ``< 1e-300``.
    """
    return "< 1e-300" if float(p) < 1e-300 else f"{float(p):.1e}"

3. Hypotheses and why we chose each test¶

# Question H₀ (nothing interesting) Hₐ Test
H1 Is zero-shot CLIP equally accurate on everyday objects and on satellite images? Same accuracy Differs Accuracy with Wilson CIs; chi-square test; recall by class
H2 Does the wording of the class sentences change the accuracy? Same accuracy for every wording Differs Four wordings on the same test images; exact McNemar tests against the plain "a photo of ..."
H3 How many labelled images per class does a linear classifier on CLIP's features need to beat zero-shot? It never does It does after a few images Learning curve from 1 to 1,000 images per class, 3 seeds
H4 Does fine-tuning beat a linear probe on the same 640 images, and does it hurt CLIP's general ability? Same accuracy; no loss Better on the new domain; worse on the old Exact McNemar test per seed; CIFAR-10 zero-shot accuracy before and after
H5 Do the approaches survive image corruptions (noise, blur, compression...)? Same accuracy as on clean images Lower, and not equally so Accuracy on 7 corrupted copies of the EuroSAT test set, with Wilson CIs

Why these tests? Every approach classifies the same test images, so we use the exact McNemar test, which compares two classifiers using only the images where they disagree. Percentages come with Wilson intervals (well behaved near 0% and 100%). Training subsets are drawn with several seeds, so the learning curve shows the spread.

4. Audit: two image sets¶

What: CIFAR-10: 60,000 tiny colour photographs of ten everyday objects (airplane, automobile, bird, cat, deer, dog, frog, horse, ship, truck). EuroSAT: 27,000 satellite tiles of ten land-use types from Sentinel-2 (forest, river, highway, crops, houses...), with seven ready-made corrupted copies of the test images (noise, blur, JPEG compression and others). CLIP reads 224 x 224 pixel images, so both sets are enlarged a lot. Why: CIFAR-10 looks like the internet photographs CLIP was trained on; EuroSAT looks like almost nothing in them. Same model, two very different tests.

Not in this project's legacy: there is no old code to replace (a new project).

How to read this:

  • CIFAR-10: 50,000 training and 10,000 test images of 32 x 32 pixels, perfectly balanced (each class is 10% of the test set).
  • EuroSAT: 21,600 training and 2,700 test images of 64 x 64 pixels; the classes are not quite balanced (7.6% to 11.7% of the test set). Its published class names are wordy ("industrial buildings or commercial buildings", "residential buildings or homes or apartments"), which matters for the prompts.
  • Seven corruptions of the test images: contrast, Gaussian noise, impulse noise, JPEG compression, motion blur, pixelation and spatter.
  • Both are enlarged 7 times (CIFAR-10) and 3.5 times (EuroSAT) to CLIP's 224 pixels, so the images the model sees are blurry.

5. CLIP in a few lines¶

What: CLIP has two towers: an image tower (a Vision Transformer, ViT-B/32) and a text tower. Each turns its input into 512 numbers, normalised to unit length, so that the cosine similarity (a dot product) between a picture and a sentence says how well they match. Zero-shot classification is then three steps: write one sentence per class, embed them (the class matrix), embed the image, and pick the class with the highest similarity. We embed the training and test images of both datasets once (up to 1,000 training images per class) and reuse them. Why: with embeddings in hand, zero-shot classification, linear probes and most of the experiments cost almost nothing.

In [3]:
processor = CLIPProcessor.from_pretrained(CLIP_NAME)
clip = CLIPModel.from_pretrained(CLIP_NAME).to(DEVICE).eval()
n_params = sum(p.numel() for p in clip.parameters()) / 1e6
n_vision = sum(p.numel() for p in clip.vision_model.parameters()) / 1e6
print(
    f"CLIP ViT-B/32: {n_params:.0f} million weights ({n_vision:.0f} million in the image tower); "
    f"images and text both become {clip.config.projection_dim} numbers"
)


def pixels(images: list) -> torch.Tensor:
    """Resizes, crops and normalises images the way CLIP expects."""
    return processor(images=[im.convert("RGB") for im in images], return_tensors="pt")[
        "pixel_values"
    ]


@torch.no_grad()
def image_embeddings(model: CLIPModel, images: list, batch: int = 128) -> np.ndarray:
    """Unit-length CLIP embeddings of images (cosine similarity is then a dot product)."""
    out = []
    for i in range(0, len(images), batch):
        feats = model.get_image_features(pixel_values=pixels(images[i : i + batch]).to(DEVICE))
        out.append(F.normalize(feats.pooler_output, dim=-1).cpu())
    return torch.cat(out).numpy()


@torch.no_grad()
def text_embeddings(prompts: list[str]) -> np.ndarray:
    """Unit-length CLIP embeddings of sentences."""
    tokens = processor(text=prompts, return_tensors="pt", padding=True).to(DEVICE)
    feats = clip.get_text_features(**tokens).pooler_output
    return F.normalize(feats, dim=-1).cpu().numpy()


def class_matrix(names: list[str], templates: list[str]) -> np.ndarray:
    """One text embedding per class: the average over prompt templates (a 'prompt ensemble')."""
    rows = []
    for name in names:
        vectors = text_embeddings([t.format(name) for t in templates])
        mean = vectors.mean(0)
        rows.append(mean / np.linalg.norm(mean))
    return np.stack(rows)


def sample_pool(labels: np.ndarray, per_class: int, gen: np.random.Generator) -> np.ndarray:
    """Random training images, up to ``per_class`` of each class."""
    keep = [
        gen.choice(
            np.flatnonzero(labels == c), min(per_class, int((labels == c).sum())), replace=False
        )
        for c in np.unique(labels)
    ]
    return np.sort(np.concatenate(keep))


pools, embeds = {}, {}
for name, d in DATASETS.items():
    train_labels = np.array(d["train"]["label"])
    pool = sample_pool(train_labels, MAX_PER_CLASS, np.random.default_rng(SEED))
    pools[name] = pool
    embeds[name] = {
        "train": image_embeddings(clip, [d["train"][int(i)][d["image"]] for i in pool]),
        "train_labels": train_labels[pool],
        "test": image_embeddings(clip, list(d["test"][d["image"]])),
        "test_labels": np.array(d["test"]["label"]),
    }
    print(f"{name}: embedded {len(pool):,} training and {len(embeds[name]['test']):,} test images")

CLIP ViT-B/32: 151 million weights (87 million in the image tower); images and text both become 512 numbers

CIFAR-10 (everyday objects): embedded 10,000 training and 10,000 test images

EuroSAT (satellite land use): embedded 10,000 training and 2,700 test images

How to read this:

  • CLIP ViT-B/32 has 151 million weights (87 million in the image tower); images and sentences both become 512 numbers.
  • We embedded 10,000 training and 10,000 test images of CIFAR-10, and 10,000 training and 2,700 test images of EuroSAT.

6. H1: how good is zero-shot, and where?¶

What: classify every test image by the sentence "a photo of {class name}." closest to it, with no training. We report the accuracy with a Wilson interval (chance is 10%), the recall of every class, and test whether the two datasets differ. Why: the promise of zero-shot is "any class, no training"; the limit of that promise depends on the domain.

In [4]:
def wilson(hits: int, total: int) -> tuple[float, float, float]:
    """A share with its 95% Wilson interval."""
    low, high = proportion_confint(hits, total, method="wilson")
    return hits / total, low, high


PLAIN = ["a photo of {}."]
zero_shot = {}
rows = []
for name, d in DATASETS.items():
    matrix = class_matrix(d["names"], PLAIN)
    pred = (embeds[name]["test"] @ matrix.T).argmax(1)
    truth = embeds[name]["test_labels"]
    zero_shot[name] = {"pred": pred, "matrix": matrix}
    acc, low, high = wilson(int((pred == truth).sum()), len(truth))
    rows.append(
        {
            "dataset": name,
            "accuracy": acc,
            "ci_low": low,
            "ci_high": high,
            "chance": 1 / len(d["names"]),
        }
    )
    recall = pd.Series(
        [(pred[truth == c] == c).mean() for c in range(len(d["names"]))], index=d["names"]
    )
    zero_shot[name]["recall"] = recall
zs_table = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("dataset")
print(
    "Zero-shot: the model has never seen a training image of these datasets; it only reads "
    "the class names inside the sentence 'a photo of {name}.'"
)
print(zs_table.round(3).to_string())
for name in DATASETS:
    r = zero_shot[name]["recall"].sort_values()
    print(
        f"\n{name}, recall by class: lowest "
        + ", ".join(f"{k} {v:.0%}" for k, v in r.head(3).items())
        + "; highest "
        + ", ".join(f"{k} {v:.0%}" for k, v in r.tail(3)[::-1].items())
    )
(a1, a2) = (zs_table["accuracy"].iloc[0], zs_table["accuracy"].iloc[1])
n1, n2 = len(embeds[list(DATASETS)[0]]["test"]), len(embeds[list(DATASETS)[1]]["test"])
chi = stats.chi2_contingency([[a1 * n1, (1 - a1) * n1], [a2 * n2, (1 - a2) * n2]])
print(f"\nCIFAR-10 minus EuroSAT: {(a1 - a2) * 100:+.1f} points (chi-square p = {fmt_p(chi[1])})")

EuroSAT (satellite land use)     0.399   0.380    0.417     0.1

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 5), layout="constrained")
for ax, (name, d) in zip(axes, DATASETS.items(), strict=True):
    recall = zero_shot[name]["recall"].sort_values()
    ax.barh(range(len(recall)), recall * 100, color=[TEAL if v >= 0.5 else ORANGE for v in recall])
    ax.set_yticks(range(len(recall)), [n[:30] for n in recall.index], fontsize=8)

    ax.set_xlim(0, 100)

    "Zero-shot CLIP is excellent on everyday objects and unreliable on satellite images",
    x=0.01,

How to read this:

  • On everyday objects zero-shot CLIP is very good: 88.8% on CIFAR-10 (95% CI 88.2% to 89.4%) without seeing a single CIFAR-10 training image. Even the weakest classes are around 80% (deer 80%, frog 80%, cat 81%) and the best near 95% (horse 97%, truck 95%, ship 94%).
  • On satellite images it is unreliable: 39.9% on EuroSAT (CI 38.0% to 41.7%), four times chance but far from usable. 49.0 points lower than CIFAR-10 (chi-square p below 1e-300). We reject H₀.
  • The failures are specific: two classes get 0% recall (pasture land and annual crop land) and river only 8%; the strong ones are residential buildings (95%), permanent crop land (81%) and lake or sea (71%). The model mixes classes whose names are close ("annual crop land" and "permanent crop land": the second one wins almost always). Zero-shot only works as well as the words and the pictures are linked in what CLIP saw during training.

7. H2: do the words matter?¶

What: the same images and the same model, four ways of writing the class sentences: the bare class name ("forest"), the plain "a photo of ...", an ensemble of six generic prompts (we embed several sentences per class and average them) and a domain-aware ensemble ("a satellite photo of ...", "an aerial photograph of ..." for EuroSAT; "a low resolution photo of a ..." for CIFAR-10). We compare each with the plain prompt with an exact McNemar test. Why: this is called prompt engineering: the model's accuracy depends on the sentence, and the sentence costs nothing to change.

In [6]:
GENERIC = [
    "{}.",
    "a photo of {}.",
    "a photo of a {}.",
    "a blurry photo of {}.",
    "a low resolution photo of {}.",
    "a close-up photo of {}.",
]
DOMAIN = {
    "CIFAR-10 (everyday objects)": [
        "a photo of a {}.",
        "a low resolution photo of a {}.",
        "a blurry photo of a {}.",
        "a photo of the small {}.",
        "a cropped photo of a {}.",
    ],
    "EuroSAT (satellite land use)": [
        "a satellite photo of {}.",
        "an aerial photograph of {}.",
        "a centered satellite photo of {}.",
        "satellite imagery of {}.",
        "an overhead view of {}.",
    ],
}
PROMPTS = {
    "bare class name": ["{}"],
    "'a photo of ...'": PLAIN,
    "ensemble of six generic prompts": GENERIC,
}
rows, preds = [], {}
for name, d in DATASETS.items():
    sets = {**PROMPTS, "domain-aware ensemble": DOMAIN[name]}
    truth = embeds[name]["test_labels"]
    for label, templates in sets.items():
        pred = (embeds[name]["test"] @ class_matrix(d["names"], templates).T).argmax(1)
        preds[(name, label)] = pred
        acc, low, high = wilson(int((pred == truth).sum()), len(truth))
        rows.append(
            {"dataset": name, "prompt": label, "accuracy": acc, "ci_low": low, "ci_high": high}
        )
prompt_table = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(prompt_table.pivot(index="prompt", columns="dataset", values="accuracy").round(3).to_string())
for name in DATASETS:
    truth = embeds[name]["test_labels"]
    base = preds[(name, "'a photo of ...'")] == truth
    for label in ("bare class name", "ensemble of six generic prompts", "domain-aware ensemble"):
        ok = preds[(name, label)] == truth
        mc = mcnemar(
            [
                [int((ok & base).sum()), int((ok & ~base).sum())],
                [int((~ok & base).sum()), int((~ok & ~base).sum())],
            ],
            exact=True,
        )
        print(
            f"{name}, {label} vs 'a photo of ...': {(ok.mean() - base.mean()) * 100:+.1f} points; "
            f"right only with it {int((ok & ~base).sum())}, only with the plain prompt "
            f"{int((~ok & base).sum())} (exact McNemar p = {fmt_p(mc.pvalue)})"
        )

How to read this:

Wording CIFAR-10 EuroSAT
Bare class name 87.4% 43.0%
"a photo of ..." 88.8% 39.9%
Six generic prompts 89.2% 41.6%
Domain-aware prompts 88.9% 51.2%
  • On EuroSAT the wording is worth up to 11 points: describing the images as satellite photos raises the accuracy from 39.9% to 51.2% (+11.3 points: right only with the new wording on 675 images, only with the plain one on 369; exact McNemar p = 2e-21). Even the bare name beats "a photo of ..." by +3.1 points (p = 1e-5), and the generic ensemble by +1.8 (p = 3e-5). We reject H₀.
  • On CIFAR-10 the wording hardly matters: the changes are -1.4 points (bare name), +0.3 (generic ensemble) and +0.0 (domain ensemble, p = 0.86).
  • The lesson: when the model is unsure, tell it the domain. The prompt that is best on one dataset (the bare name) is not best on another ("a photo of a ..." wins on CIFAR-10), so prompts must be tuned on labelled validation images, not guessed.

8. H3: how many labelled images beat zero-shot?¶

What: take the frozen CLIP embeddings, and train a linear probe (a logistic regression) on 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 64, 256 or 1,000 labelled images per class (3 random subsets of each size, except for the largest) and measure the test accuracy. We compare with zero-shot. Why: the real choice for a practitioner is "zero-shot now, or label some images". How many?

In [8]:
def few_shot_subset(labels: np.ndarray, shots: int, seed: int) -> np.ndarray:
    """``shots`` random training images of each class (the same for a given seed)."""
    return sample_pool(labels, shots, np.random.default_rng([SEED, seed, shots]))


def probe_accuracy(name: str, shots: int, seed: int) -> tuple[float, np.ndarray]:
    """Test accuracy of a logistic regression on frozen CLIP embeddings."""
    e = embeds[name]
    idx = few_shot_subset(e["train_labels"], shots, seed)
    model = LogisticRegression(C=10.0, max_iter=2_000).fit(e["train"][idx], e["train_labels"][idx])
    pred = model.predict(e["test"])
    return float((pred == e["test_labels"]).mean()), pred


rows = []
for name in DATASETS:
    for shots in SHOTS:
        for seed in range(N_SEEDS if shots < MAX_PER_CLASS else 1):
            rows.append(
                {
                    "dataset": name,
                    "shots": shots,
                    "seed": seed,
                    "accuracy": probe_accuracy(name, shots, seed)[0],
                }
            )
curve = pd.DataFrame(rows)
mean = curve.groupby(["dataset", "shots"])["accuracy"].agg(["mean", "std"]).round(3)
print(
    "Linear probe on frozen CLIP embeddings: test accuracy by number of labelled images per "

)
print(mean["mean"].unstack(0).to_string())
for name in DATASETS:
    zs = zs_table.loc[name, "accuracy"]
    sub = curve[curve["dataset"] == name].groupby("shots")["accuracy"].mean()
    beats = sub[sub > zs]

        f"{name}: zero-shot {zs:.3f}; the probe first beats it with "
        f"{first} labelled image(s) per class"
        if first
        else f"{name}: never beaten"
    )

Labelled images per class CIFAR-10 EuroSAT
0 (zero-shot) 88.8% 39.9%

  • On EuroSAT a single labelled image per class beats zero-shot (52.5% against 39.9%), and 16 per class reach 83%. We reject H₀.
  • On CIFAR-10 it takes 16 per class: the probe equals zero-shot at about 8 per class (88.7% against 88.8%) and overtakes it at 16 (89.9%); with one image per class it is far worse (63.1%).
  • With plenty of labels both reach about 94%: 1,000 images per class give 94.3% (CIFAR-10) and 94.6% (EuroSAT). The zero-shot advantage is mostly a label-saving advantage, and it is largest exactly where there are no labels.
  • Zero-shot is therefore the right starting point for familiar domains and a quick baseline everywhere; a handful of labelled images is the best investment for an unfamiliar one.

9. H4: what does fine-tuning buy, and what does it cost?¶

What: fine-tune CLIP's image tower on EuroSAT with only 64 labelled images per class (640 images), for 5 epochs with a small learning rate (0.00001), flips and rotations as augmentation. The classifier starts from the zero-shot class matrix (the text embeddings) and is trained together with the image tower. We compare with the linear probe trained on the same 640 images (exact McNemar test, 3 seeds). Then the cost: we test the fine-tuned image tower on CIFAR-10 zero-shot (with the original text tower) to see whether it has forgotten its general ability. Why: fine-tuning is the heavy tool; we should know what it adds beyond the probe and what it takes away.

In [10]:
euro = DATASETS["EuroSAT (satellite land use)"]
cifar_d = DATASETS["CIFAR-10 (everyday objects)"]
euro_text = torch.tensor(zero_shot["EuroSAT (satellite land use)"]["matrix"], device=DEVICE)
cifar_text = zero_shot["CIFAR-10 (everyday objects)"]["matrix"]
cifar_idx = np.random.default_rng(SEED).choice(
    len(cifar_d["test"]), CIFAR_FORGET_IMAGES, replace=False
)
cifar_images = [cifar_d["test"][int(i)]["img"] for i in cifar_idx]
cifar_truth = np.array(cifar_d["test"]["label"])[cifar_idx]
euro_train_labels = embeds["EuroSAT (satellite land use)"]["train_labels"]
euro_pool = pools["EuroSAT (satellite land use)"]
euro_test_images = list(euro["test"]["image"])
euro_test_truth = embeds["EuroSAT (satellite land use)"]["test_labels"]


def fine_tune(seed: int) -> tuple[CLIPModel, torch.Tensor]:
    """Fine-tunes CLIP's image tower on EuroSAT with ``FINE_TUNE_SHOTS`` images per class.

    The classifier is the matrix of class-name text embeddings (zero-shot weights) and is
    trained together with the image tower, so training starts from the zero-shot classifier.
    The text tower is not changed.

    Args:
        seed: Seed for the training subset, the order of the batches and the augmentation.

    Returns:
        The fine-tuned model and the trained classifier matrix.
    """
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    model = CLIPModel.from_pretrained(CLIP_NAME).to(DEVICE)
    head = torch.nn.Parameter(euro_text.clone().float())
    params = list(model.vision_model.parameters()) + list(model.visual_projection.parameters())
    optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(
        [{"params": params, "lr": LEARNING_RATE}, {"params": [head], "lr": LEARNING_RATE * 10}],
        weight_decay=0.1,
    )
    idx = few_shot_subset(euro_train_labels, FINE_TUNE_SHOTS, seed)
    images = [euro["train"][int(euro_pool[i])]["image"] for i in idx]
    labels = torch.tensor(euro_train_labels[idx], device=DEVICE)
    x = pixels(images)
    steps = EPOCHS * int(np.ceil(len(idx) / BATCH))
    scheduler = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.CosineAnnealingLR(optimizer, steps)
    gen = torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed)
    model.train()
    for _ in range(EPOCHS):
        order = torch.randperm(len(idx), generator=gen)
        for start in range(0, len(idx), BATCH):
            pick = order[start : start + BATCH]
            batch = x[pick].to(DEVICE)
            if torch.rand(1, generator=gen).item() < 0.5:
                batch = batch.flip(-1)
            batch = torch.rot90(batch, int(torch.randint(0, 4, (1,), generator=gen)), (2, 3))
            feats = F.normalize(model.get_image_features(pixel_values=batch).pooler_output, dim=-1)
            logits = 100.0 * feats @ F.normalize(head, dim=-1).T
            loss = F.cross_entropy(logits, labels[pick])
            optimizer.zero_grad()
            loss.backward()
            optimizer.step()
            scheduler.step()
    return model.eval(), head.detach()


@torch.no_grad()
def classify_with(
    model: CLIPModel, head: torch.Tensor, images: list, batch: int = 128
) -> np.ndarray:
    """Predicted EuroSAT classes from a (fine-tuned) model and classifier matrix."""
    feats = image_embeddings(model, images, batch)
    return (
        (torch.tensor(feats, device=DEVICE) @ F.normalize(head, dim=-1).T).argmax(1).cpu().numpy()
    )


@torch.no_grad()
def cifar_zero_shot(model: CLIPModel) -> float:
    """CIFAR-10 zero-shot accuracy of a model's image tower with the original text tower."""
    feats = image_embeddings(model, cifar_images)
    return float(((feats @ cifar_text.T).argmax(1) == cifar_truth).mean())


rows, kept = [], {}
base_cifar = cifar_zero_shot(clip)
for seed in range(N_SEEDS):
    model, head = fine_tune(seed)
    pred = classify_with(model, head, euro_test_images)
    probe_acc, probe_pred = probe_accuracy("EuroSAT (satellite land use)", FINE_TUNE_SHOTS, seed)
    rows.append(
        {
            "seed": seed,
            "zero-shot": zs_table.loc["EuroSAT (satellite land use)", "accuracy"],
            "linear probe": probe_acc,
            "fine-tuned": float((pred == euro_test_truth).mean()),
            "CIFAR-10 zero-shot after": cifar_zero_shot(model),
            "CIFAR-10 zero-shot before": base_cifar,
        }
    )
    ok_ft, ok_probe = pred == euro_test_truth, probe_pred == euro_test_truth
    mc = mcnemar(
        [
            [int((ok_ft & ok_probe).sum()), int((ok_ft & ~ok_probe).sum())],
            [int((~ok_ft & ok_probe).sum()), int((~ok_ft & ~ok_probe).sum())],
        ],
        exact=True,
    )
    rows[-1]["McNemar p, fine-tuned vs probe"] = mc.pvalue
    if seed == 0:
        kept = {"model": model, "head": head, "pred": pred}
    else:
        del model
        torch.cuda.empty_cache()
ft = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("seed")
shown = ft.copy()
shown["McNemar p, fine-tuned vs probe"] = shown["McNemar p, fine-tuned vs probe"].map(fmt_p)
print(
    f"EuroSAT with {FINE_TUNE_SHOTS} labelled images per class ({FINE_TUNE_SHOTS * 10} images), "
    f"{EPOCHS} epochs:"
)
print(shown.round(3).to_string())
print(
    f"\nMean over {N_SEEDS} seeds: zero-shot {ft['zero-shot'].mean():.3f}, linear probe "
    f"{ft['linear probe'].mean():.3f}, fine-tuned {ft['fine-tuned'].mean():.3f}"
)
after = ft["CIFAR-10 zero-shot after"].mean()
print(
    f"CIFAR-10 zero-shot accuracy of the fine-tuned model: {after:.3f} against "
    f"{base_cifar:.3f} before fine-tuning on satellite images "
    f"({(after - base_cifar) * 100:+.1f} points)"
)

EuroSAT with 64 labelled images per class (640 images), 5 epochs:
      zero-shot  linear probe  fine-tuned  CIFAR-10 zero-shot after  CIFAR-10 zero-shot before McNemar p, fine-tuned vs probe
seed                                                                                                                         
0         0.399         0.889       0.959                     0.750                      0.894                        5.5e-31
1         0.399         0.884       0.954                     0.718                      0.894                        1.0e-30
2         0.399         0.888       0.966                     0.762                      0.894                        1.8e-40

Mean over 3 seeds: zero-shot 0.399, linear probe 0.887, fine-tuned 0.960

How to read this:

  • Fine-tuning is clearly the best on the new domain: with 640 images the fine-tuned model reaches 96.0% (95.9%, 95.4%, 96.6% over the three seeds), against 88.7% for the linear probe on the same images and 39.9% for zero-shot. It beats the probe in every seed (exact McNemar p from 1e-30 to 1e-40). We reject H₀.
  • But it forgets what it knew: the same fine-tuned image tower scores only 74.3% on CIFAR-10 zero-shot (75.0%, 71.8%, 76.2%), against 89.4% before: -15.1 points (about one in six everyday photographs newly misclassified), although it never saw a CIFAR-10 image and its text tower is unchanged. This is catastrophic forgetting: training pulls the image embeddings towards satellite classes and away from the shared space the text tower speaks.
  • The trade-off is real: a fine-tuned model is a specialist. If it must keep its general ability, use the linear probe (frozen features, nothing forgotten) or a gentler method (fewer steps, a smaller learning rate, or mixing the fine-tuned and original weights).

10. H5: how robust is each approach?¶

What: the EuroSAT test images come with seven corrupted copies (contrast change, Gaussian and impulse noise, JPEG compression, motion blur, pixelation, spatter). We classify them with the three approaches trained on clean images (zero-shot with the plain prompt; the linear probe and the fine-tuned model of seed 0, both trained on the same 640 clean images) and compare the accuracy. Why: a model that is excellent on a tidy test set and collapses on a dirty camera is a trap.

The drilled student, trained on clean tiles, is more thrown by sensor noise than the one who only learned a light classifier on top of general features. We reject H₀ for all three methods; the ranking depends on the corruption.
  • The lesson: accuracy on a clean test set says little about a dirty camera; test with the corruptions you expect.

11. 🎯 Takeaways¶

  1. Zero-shot works where the pictures look like the internet: 88.8% on CIFAR-10 with no training image; 39.9% on satellite tiles (a 49-point gap).
  2. The words matter most when the model is unsure: satellite-aware prompts lift EuroSAT from 39.9% to 51.2% (+11.3 points, p = 2e-21); on CIFAR-10 they change nothing.
  3. A few labelled images beat zero-shot in an unfamiliar domain: one image per class on EuroSAT (52.5% against 39.9%), 16 on CIFAR-10; with 1,000 per class both reach about 94%.
  4. Fine-tuning is the strongest tool and a specialist's trap: 96.0% on EuroSAT from 640 images, against 88.7% for the probe, but CIFAR-10 zero-shot falls from 89.4% to 74.3% (catastrophic forgetting).
  5. No approach survives corruption unscathed: the probe loses 46 points on average, the fine-tuned model 44 (and it is worse than the probe under noise).
  6. Zero-shot is a baseline, not a product: use it to start, to choose what to label, and to compare against.

12. ⚠️ Limitations¶

  • One CLIP model (ViT-B/32, the smallest of the popular ones). Larger CLIP models, and newer ones trained on more or cleaner data, are better and may be more robust.
  • Two small-image datasets. CIFAR-10 and EuroSAT images are 32 or 64 pixels and are enlarged, which hurts every method; results on full-size photographs would differ.
  • Prompt sets were written by hand and tried once; the domain-aware gain depends on the wording and was not tuned on a validation set.
  • The linear probe uses one regularisation setting (C = 10) for every training size; with one image per class a tuned setting could do better.
  • Fine-tuning used one recipe (64 images per class, 5 epochs, learning rate 0.00001, no tuning), and the forgetting measure is CIFAR-10 zero-shot on 3,000 test images; gentler recipes forget less.
  • The robustness test uses the seed-0 models only, and corruptions were applied to the test images, not the training images (training with noise would likely repair the noise result).
  • No fairness or safety review: CLIP inherits the biases of its internet training data, and zero-shot class names such as people-related labels can behave badly; none of that is measured here.
  • EuroSAT's class names are awkward ("annual crop land" against "permanent crop land"), so some zero-shot failures reflect the labelling scheme more than the model.
